The computational domain consists of a modern 10-stage industrial axial compressor, with each stage comprising a row of rotor blades and a row of stator blades.
The full computational mesh has over 15 million nodes.
The data is pre-processed to extract only the relevant engineering data, reducing the dimensionality from over 15 million nodes to around 100,000 nodes.
The neural network architecture is based on a 3D U-Net with double residual convolutional blocks.
The input to the model includes the tip clearance, surface roughness, and blade geometry parameters.
The output of the model is a tensor of size (6x24x64x64) representing the 3D flow field variables.
The dataset is divided into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% hold-out data.
The model is trained using the AdamW optimizer and Huber loss function.
The training is performed with 5 different random seeds, and the results are reported as the mean and standard deviation of the losses.
The final model showed a training loss of (1.29 ± 0.16)·10^-3 and a test loss of (1.96 ± 0.40)·10^-3 (Huber Loss ± standard deviation).
The tip clearance and surface roughness were varied for each blade row within out-of-tolerance conditions up to 50% larger and tighter than the drawing specifications.
The proposed C(NN)FD architecture is proven to achieve an accuracy comparable to that of the CFD benchmark, in real-time, for an industrially relevant application.
The C(NN)FD framework provides explainability to the overall performance predictions by identifying the corresponding aerodynamic drivers.

The C(NN)FD framework is readily integrated within the manufacturing and build process of gas turbines, providing the opportunity to analytically assess the impact on performance with actionable and explainable data.
The C(NN)FD framework reduces the requirements for expensive physical tests by avoiding the high computational costs and long lead times of traditional CFD analyses.
